params.title: The Fourier Transform
params.subtitle: From time domain to frequency domain

beats.caption: The Fourier Transform
beats.narration: Welcome. Today we explore how any signal can be broken down into its underlying frequencies.

beats.caption: A signal built from two waves
beats.narration: Imagine a sound wave made by adding two simpler waves together. Each one has its own frequency and strength.

beats.caption: Two waves add into one signal
beats.narration: When waves overlap, their heights add at every instant. That is superposition, and it creates the combined signal you see.

beats.caption: Frequency domain shows two peaks
beats.narration: In the frequency domain, the same signal appears as two distinct peaks, one for each ingredient frequency.

beats.caption: The Fourier transform
beats.narration: The Fourier transform converts a time signal into a function of frequency, revealing how much of each frequency is present.

beats.caption: The inverse Fourier transform
beats.narration: The inverse transform does the opposite, rebuilding the original time signal from its frequency ingredients.

right.heading: FFT
bullets: Cost grows as N log N

beats.caption: DFT and FFT give the same result
beats.narration: The discrete Fourier transform handles sampled signals directly. The FFT is a clever algorithm that produces the same output with far fewer operations.

params.value: O(N squared) to O(N log N)
params.label: FFT complexity reduction

beats.caption: FFT cuts the cost dramatically
beats.narration: For large data sets, dropping from N squared to N log N means the difference between minutes and milliseconds.
